entries.section: (1) Paul's greeting and his defense of his apostleship

paragraphs.text: Not of men, neither by man: that is, he was not a disciple at the hands of any human being, and no man sent him to preach. But by Jesus Christ, and God the Father: as one single source of the mission, for the Father and the Son are one in essence. This is a confession of the divinity of Christ, since St. Paul affirms that He (Christ) is not of men, that is, He is not an ordinary man.

Who raised him from the dead: the resurrection of Christ from the dead is ascribed sometimes to the Father and sometimes to Christ Himself. If St. Paul ascribed it to the Father here, we must not forget that Christ said of His death and resurrection, "I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again" (Jn 10:18). St. Paul begins his epistle in a severe tone, unlike his custom, by identifying himself and his apostleship, which is from the Lord Christ Himself, like all the apostles and disciples whom Christ sent during His incarnation. He declares that he was not sent by the apostles or by any human source, in order to answer those who cast doubt on his apostleship on the pretext that he had not seen Christ on earth and was therefore lesser in standing and in the worth of what he teaches. They did this in order to spread their strange teachings about the necessity of circumcision, of becoming Jews, and of submitting to the works of the Law.

entries.section: (1) Paul's greeting and his defense of his apostleship

paragraphs.text: The churches of Galatia: Galatia was a province or region that included several churches. It was not one city or one church, but several churches scattered in some cities such as "Ancyra" and "Thafium", and the strange teachings had spread throughout the whole region. He sends them greetings in his own name and in the name of those who were with him in the ministry at that time.

entries.section: (1) Paul's greeting and his defense of his apostleship

paragraphs.text: Grace be to you and peace: he wishes them the work of God's grace within them, and especially the peace that fills their hearts.
Our Father: that is, through redemption we received the grace of adoption.
That he might deliver us from this present evil world: we are no longer enslaved to sin.

The Apostle Paul shows the oneness of the Father and the Son in essence as the source of grace and peace. Although the Son offered the redemption, it was accomplished according to the will of the Father. Thus he shows the oneness of will between the Father and the Son, and shows by this that salvation is by the blood of Christ, and not by the works of the Law as the false teachers proclaim.

entries.section: (1) Paul's greeting and his defense of his apostleship

paragraphs.text: The Apostle concludes the introduction by offering glory to God, for He is worthy of glory and honor forever..
Do we always give glory and thanks to God for the grace of redemption and adoption, and because He keeps us every day from the evils of this present world so that we may be with Him in eternity?!

entries.section: (2) Rejecting false teachings and anathema on those who follow them

paragraphs.text: So soon: the Galatians believed and were baptized six years before the writing of this epistle, when Paul visited them on his first journey, and likewise on his second journey, three years ago, they were holding fast to the sound faith. So their change took place a short time before the writing of this epistle, and the Apostle marvels that they were influenced by the teaching of the false teachers and left the faith in which they had lived for about five years.
Another gospel: another, different message, that is, the teachings of the false teachers.

In his epistles, after the introduction, St. Paul was accustomed to give thanks to God for those to whom he was writing. Here, however, he begins with a sharp rebuke because of the gravity of turning away from the right faith, for it is a matter of life or death. Yet he gives them hope of repentance: he does not say, "You have been removed, and it is finished," but "you are removed," that is, they can still repent, return, and stand firm in the faith. He expresses astonishment at the swiftness of their turning, when they had believed at his hands by the call of God, who called them to the grace of Christ to receive redemption and free salvation, to another call, to salvation by the works of the Law and circumcision.

entries.section: (2) Rejecting false teachings and anathema on those who follow them

paragraphs.text: Which is not another: that is, it is not a gospel at all, and those who proclaim it trouble you, for there is only one Gospel. Even if the four Evangelists wrote it, its meaning and its message are one, whereas a single man may write a book that contradicts itself.

entries.section: (2) Rejecting false teachings and anathema on those who follow them

paragraphs.text: If we preach: here Paul places himself in the rank of the apostles, and says that his message is the very same Gospel as that of the rest of the apostles. The false teachers claimed that after Paul had preached to Galatia he changed his teaching. So here he pronounces anathema on himself if he had changed his preaching as the false teachers accuse him, in order to confirm the true message about Christ which he preached to them.
An angel from heaven: Satan, who can change his form into the likeness of an angel of light (2 Cor 11:14). Than that which we have preached: that is, what you received.
Accursed (anathema): that is, excommunicated.

Here Paul uses the authority of binding and loosing, as the Lord delivered it to His disciples. For this reason St. Paul stressed faithfulness in handing down the faith (2 Tim 1:13), (1 Cor 11:23), (2 Tim 2:2). The Coptic Orthodox Church has offered thousands of martyrs to preserve what she received of the sound faith, so we must hold fast to the faith that we received from the Fathers. We note that apostolic authority was not for boasting but for edification (2 Cor 10:8). And Paul places himself within the circle of anathema if he should change his faith. By this he makes clear that he does not despise the message of the rest of the apostles, but that the Christian message has one source, which is the Holy Spirit.

entries.section: (2) Rejecting false teachings and anathema on those who follow them

paragraphs.text: Paul used to please men in all things, even at his own expense: "Even as I please all men in all things, not seeking mine own profit" (1 Cor 10:33). But when the matter concerns faith and doctrine, he does not yield and shows no readiness for leniency, for he submits to the truth that is in Christ because he is the servant of Christ and not of men.

Do we please God or men?..! Pilate was sure of the innocence of Christ, but he pleased the people and handed Him over to them to be crucified. Everyone who pleases men at the expense of God tramples on the right of Christ. Paul endured very many sufferings that he could have avoided had he said what pleases men, but he was careful to preserve the soundness of the faith that is pleasing to Christ.

entries.section: (3) Paul's calling and his life before the faith

paragraphs.text: The Apostle defends the truth of the Gospel that he preaches, and says that he did not receive his teachings from a man but by the revelation of Jesus Christ Himself, and this is sufficient proof of the truth of his message. This must have happened directly from the Lord during the period of his retreat in the Arabian desert near Damascus, after he saw the Lord (v. 17).

entries.section: (3) Paul's calling and his life before the faith

paragraphs.text: Beyond measure: that is, without mercy.
Wasted it: that is, destroyed it and scattered the believers in it, harming them in every way, even to the point of killing.
My equals: that is, those of his own age among the children of Israel.

The Apostle Paul reminds them of his former conduct, and how he was a Jew zealous for the teachings of Moses, and advanced in the learning of the Jewish religion because he had studied at the feet of the greatest teacher of the Law, Gamaliel (Acts 22:3, Phil 3:5, 1 Tim 1:13). He does this in order to show the power of divine grace in his life, since he had been a greater persecutor of the Christians than his equals. But when the Lord Jesus called him, he turned with all his energy to building the Church of Christ, after he had been working to destroy it. He had been a Jewish religious leader, fanatical for the Pharisaic traditions of the Law, but after he came to know the truth he turned completely to defending Christianity and preaching it.

Be ready to hear the other opinion, and God will guide you, however far you have strayed, and you will return to the truth. Do not neglect the opinion of others or interrupt them, but pray while you listen to them, and you will learn from everyone and grow in wisdom from God day by day.

entries.section: (4) Paul's life after accepting the faith

paragraphs.text: Separated me from my mother's womb: his calling was from his mother's womb, by the foreknowledge of God who set him apart for a special mission, as He set apart John the Baptist from his mother's womb.

That I might preach him among the heathen (the Gentiles): Paul's preaching was focused on the lands of the world filled with the Gentiles, and he did not preach in Judea. But this does not mean that he did not preach to the few Jews living among the Gentiles; rather, he cared for them because they had the prophecies about Christ, and they helped him in his ministry in many countries.

Truly a change took place in the life of the Apostle Paul as he was on the way to Damascus, when he was going to persecute the Church of Christ. When God revealed Himself to Paul, he accepted the call, and it pleased God to reveal His Son in him. St. John Chrysostom says that Paul said "to reveal his Son in me" and did not say "to me", in order to show that he did not receive the faith by words alone but by the work of the Holy Spirit in him: "I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me" (Gal 2:20). So his life and his conduct were changed.

Immediately: Paul accepted the call and went out to the desert (east of the Jordan) and stayed there three years for prayer and retreat, for studying the prophecies about Christ, for reviewing what he had studied, and for seeking God's counsel. In his humility he did not mention this in his epistle, and said:

I conferred not with flesh and blood: he is being careful because of those who cast doubt on his apostleship, so he affirms that his calling was from Christ directly and that he sought the counsel of no one, but went straight to his retreat in the desert. St. Paul shows that when God called him on his way to Damascus, he believed and was baptized, and then went out to the Arabian desert near Damascus in retreat for three years, in which he received from Christ all the teachings, so that he became an apostle of His like the rest of the twelve disciples.

entries.section: (4) Paul's life after accepting the faith

paragraphs.text: Them which were apostles before me: the gathering of the apostles and the center of the preaching was in Jerusalem, and Paul did not go to them to consult them. Here he declares that he is an apostle, and that the disciples of Christ were apostles before him.
Arabia: a desert near the city of Damascus in Syria, which is different from the Arabian peninsula or the desert of Sinai.
Damascus: an ancient city that still has the same name today, as the capital of Syria.

Although Paul stayed some days in Damascus after Ananias baptized him, he did not go up to Jerusalem but went out into the wilderness, and returned with a burning, fiery heart after receiving his teachings from the Lord Himself.

entries.section: (4) Paul's life after accepting the faith

paragraphs.text: Three years: counted from his baptism at the hands of Ananias; he spent them in the Arabian desert, then returned to Damascus for a short time and went from there to Jerusalem.

When Paul went up to Jerusalem to become acquainted with Peter, he stayed there only 15 days, and met with James, whom he mentions with reverence, saying "the Lord's brother". He was the son of Mary the wife of Clopas and the sister of the Virgin Mary, and was bishop of Jerusalem. He did not meet any of the other apostles, because they were preaching outside Jerusalem. Thus he declares that he was not working alone, but in a spirit not separate from the leadership of the Church. And he was not hasty to meet the Apostle Peter right after his baptism, because the field of his preaching was among the Gentiles and not among the Jews like Peter, as Christ declared to him (Acts 22:17-21).

entries.section: (4) Paul's life after accepting the faith

paragraphs.text: The Apostle Paul went on to serve in Antioch and Cilicia (Tarsus, his homeland) to preach among the Gentiles. He did not go up to Jerusalem to learn from Peter, but to become acquainted with him. And he says the truth, with God as his witness, that he does not lie.

entries.section: (4) Paul's life after accepting the faith

paragraphs.text: St. Paul humbly mentions his former errors, and how the churches of Jewish origin accepted him after his conversion even though they had not seen him before, but had only heard of his past and his cruelty in persecuting the Christians.

entries.section: (4) Paul's life after accepting the faith

paragraphs.text: The believers in the churches of Judea used to pray for him, and God answered their petition, so they glorified God because of His work in Paul's life. His acceptance of God's call had as its result that he said, "God reveals ... in me ... they glorified God in me."

The Lord Christ commanded us, "That they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven" (Mt 5:16). Are we like that?... If the Church offers glorification to God on the feasts of the saints because Christ lived in them and appeared by His light and teachings in their practical lives, does our life glorify God or cause others to stumble?! And do we pray for our repentance and the repentance of others so that God may be glorified in us?.!
Paul's defense of his apostleship

entries.section: (1) Paul presents his message to the council of Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: Fourteen years: this is most probably counted from the time of the calling of the Apostle Paul, and so this is not his first journey to Jerusalem, which was in the year 38 A.D. (Acts 9:26-30). Barnabas: the meaning of his name is son of exhortation (Acts 4:36); he was known for generosity, and he knew Paul and accompanied him on his first journey.
Titus: of Greek origin, one of Paul's disciples and companions.

Paul went to Jerusalem to present his message to the apostles, because of the false teachers who cast doubt on his apostleship and proclaimed the necessity of circumcision and the works of the Law for those converted from among the Gentiles.

entries.section: (1) Paul presents his message to the council of Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: Privately: Paul met in secret with the pillars of the Church, who were James the brother of the Lord, bishop of Jerusalem, and Peter and John, and then met with the whole council, which included the rest of the apostles and the priests (Acts 15:6). He met first with the three who were of reputation so that it would be easier to persuade the large council that included the apostles and the priests. All these meetings were held on a limited scale so as not to stir up the Jews in Jerusalem.

In vain: Paul does not doubt his preaching, because Christ is the One who taught him it. But by "in vain" he means that his preaching might be wrong in the eyes of the apostles. So he wanted to present what he preaches and obtain their agreement to it, so that the false teachers would not cast doubt on what he teaches.

Paul's movements were always by heavenly revelation and under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, and for this reason we find him at one time saying that the Spirit forbade them. This is the life of the saints, who move by God's guidance and not out of enthusiasm for some idea. And the Holy Spirit gathered in Jerusalem the four pillars of the Church, Peter, James (the brother of the Lord), John, and Paul, to arrange the preaching in the whole world (v. 9). Paul represented the door opened wide for receiving the Gentiles into the faith. So this council, that is, the council of Jerusalem in the year 50 A.D., was the oldest historical document of the early Church, among the apostolic canons, concerning the acceptance of the Gentiles.

entries.section: (1) Paul presents his message to the council of Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: The wisdom of the Apostle Paul led him to take with him his disciple Titus the Greek, and he openly declared that he was not circumcised. None of the pillars of the Church opposed him; rather, their opinions were united in not obliging the Gentiles to circumcision or the ordinances of the Law. On the contrary, they supported Paul, although he had circumcised Timothy so that the Jews would accept him to preach among them, and not out of a belief that circumcision was necessary.

entries.section: (1) Paul presents his message to the council of Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: False brethren brought in: that is, Satan brought them in, as tares are sown among the wheat, with the aim of dividing the Church.
Privily: in secret, so as to be like moths that eat away the holy building and nullify the liberty which is in Christ.

Here Paul explains the reason for his going to Jerusalem and the purpose of his preaching, which is to refute the opinions of the false teachers, who cast doubt on his preaching and hinder the growth of the Church. For these teachers proclaim the necessity of circumcision and the works of the Law, so that they would enslave the Christians of Gentile origin to these symbolic matters and nullify their freedom in life with Christ, which does not need these matters, since the sacraments of the Church and the means of grace, such as prayers and fasts ... etc., have taken their place.

entries.section: (1) Paul presents his message to the council of Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: We gave place (we yielded): we surrendered.

Paul stood against them with courage and showed no compliance or appeasement, and firmly rejected what they proclaim, in order to preserve the right of the Gospel in the freedom that is in Christ by the work of grace: "knowing that I am set for the defence of the gospel" (Phil 1:17). We see Paul elsewhere agreeing to the circumcision of Timothy so that he could win the Jews to Christianity, because he was of Jewish origin. Thus the Holy Spirit guides us to act in a way that does not cause the ministry to stumble.

The Church believes in the opinion of the council, that is, the council of bishops, to lead the Church, and likewise the council of the priests and servants who guide their church, so that she does not act on a private opinion without returning to those in authority. If you are in authority, take care to obtain the agreement of the other leaders, so that you keep the peace of the ministry and stay away from divisions, because peace within the Church is more important than any project or new idea that disturbs the Church.

entries.section: (2) Paul, the apostle of the Gentiles

paragraphs.text: Those who seemed to be somewhat: they are the pillars of the Church, that is, James, Peter and John.
Man's person: that is, looking at a man's position and fame.

Paul did not diminish the dignity of those who seemed to be somewhat, but equates his apostleship with theirs: "For in nothing am I behind the very chiefest apostles, though I be nothing" (2 Cor 12:11). That is, all the glory returns to the work of God in the Church: "But by the grace of God I am what I am ... but the grace of God which was with me" (1 Cor 15:10). So there is no difference between one apostle and another, whatever his standing, because the One working in them all is the Holy Spirit. For this reason none of the apostles advised him anything contrary to his preaching, because he had received it by revelation directly from Christ; on the contrary, they approved of his preaching and their opinions agreed together. If Paul defends his apostleship, it is to establish the right faith and not for the sake of his personal honor.

entries.section: (2) Paul, the apostle of the Gentiles

paragraphs.text: Gospel: a message, or preaching.
The uncircumcision: the absence of circumcision, by which the Gentiles are meant.
The circumcision: by which the Jews are meant.
Was committed: it appeared from the guidance of the Holy Spirit to Paul and his preaching among the Gentiles that God had entrusted him and directed him to the ministry of the Gentiles.

James: he is the brother of the Lord, that is, the son of Alphaeus, one of the disciples of Christ, and he was bishop of Jerusalem; as for James the son of Zebedee, Herod had killed him (Acts 12:2). Cephas: Peter.
John: the son of Zebedee.

The apostles, the pillars of the Church, who are Peter, James and John, rejoiced in Paul's zeal and supported him by sending Barnabas with him, "the right hands of fellowship." The right hand of fellowship means a handshake with the right hand, signifying sharing in one ministry, that is, that he might support him in preaching among the Gentiles. Their support was strong, because it came from those who were of reputation among the Jews. This is the spirit of Christian ministry: there is no jealousy among the saints, because the goal is one, which is the salvation of the peoples, and the One working in them is one, who is the Holy Spirit and not the human self. Therefore we find John the Baptist saying of Christ, "He must increase, but I must decrease" (Jn 3:30).

entries.section: (2) Paul, the apostle of the Gentiles

paragraphs.text: None of the pillars of the Church advised Paul anything except to help the poor of Jerusalem at the time of the famine, since Herod had begun by killing James the brother of John with the sword, imprisoning Peter, and mistreating the Christians (Acts 12).

May we review the goal of our life: do we live for ourselves, or is our goal the glory of Christ and the spread of His Kingdom?! Then we will feel for those around us and try to help them with all our strength.

entries.section: (3) Paul's confrontation with Peter

paragraphs.text: Antioch: Antioch of Syria, which is different from Antioch of Pisidia.
I withstood him: I rebuked him.
Certain came from James: Christians of Jewish origin from Jerusalem, whose bishop was James the brother of the Lord.

Peter went to Antioch after that, and was eating with Paul and with the Christians of Gentile origin, but when Christians of Jewish origin came, Peter withdrew himself out of shame before them, lest he cause them to stumble. So the Apostle Paul stood against him, because this error was not personal, but also brought down others behind him into the sin of hypocrisy. We see here that Paul was courageous, while Peter, and behind him Barnabas and some of the Christians of Jewish origin who were in Antioch, were ashamed to declare that the Christians of Gentile origin are the same as the Christians of Jewish origin, and that they are not required to have circumcision and the Law in order to receive salvation. So they did not eat with the Christians of Gentile origin in front of the Christians of Jewish origin, as if they were declaring the uncleanness of the Christians of Gentile origin, or that they were eating foods that Christianity does not approve, although Christianity has no forbidden foods as Judaism does, which forbade some foods for the sake of spiritual symbols that ended with the appearing of Christianity.

entries.section: (3) Paul's confrontation with Peter

paragraphs.text: They walked not uprightly: that is, they walked in hypocrisy.

Paul considered that the conduct of Peter and Barnabas was not according to the uprightness of the Gospel, because by this conduct they regard the Gentiles as sinners. And if Peter, who is of Jewish origin, lives without being bound by the Law, as is proved by his eating with the Gentiles of the foods forbidden to the Jews, why does he compel the Gentiles to live as Jews, that is, to keep the Law?

Some of the Fathers, such as St. John Chrysostom and St. Jerome, see that this action of Peter was by arrangement with Paul, to give an opportunity for Paul to rebuke him and for him to be silent, so that the Jews would be assured that compelling the Gentiles to live as Jews is wrong.

Do not be afraid to declare the truth, whatever the standing of those who oppose, especially if their conduct causes others to stumble. Ask God's help to give you wisdom in speech, so that you win everyone. And if someone is troubled, you will win him by love after a while, but do not yield the truth for the sake of God.

entries.section: (4) Justification by Christ and not by the works of the Law

paragraphs.text: God forbid: an expression of denial, meaning strong rejection.

Paul continues his speech with Peter and says to him: If we, who were born Jews, and not Gentile idolaters, did not benefit from this privilege, since we were not justified by the works of the Law such as circumcision and keeping the Sabbath, but the Law pronounced a sentence of death upon us, then we are sinners like the Gentiles, and therefore we turned to faith in Christ, because Christ is the source of justification and faith in Him is the means of obtaining justification, whereas the works of the Law are not a source of justification. After we have turned to faith in Christ to be justified, do we return to the Law again?! This return would mean that Christ did not justify me, but pushed me to disobey the Law and so caused me to fall into sin, that is, He was a minister of sin, and thereby I place Christ under bondage to the Law "as a minister of sin", that is, the cause of my committing it. God forbid that Christ should be a minister of sin, for the Law was a master over us, taking occasion from sin to pronounce on us the sentence of death as slaves of sin.

entries.section: (4) Justification by Christ and not by the works of the Law

paragraphs.text: If I build again the works of the Law, that is, circumcision and living as a Jew, which I had destroyed, I make myself a transgressor, because Christ broke down the wall of partition that was between the Jews and the Gentiles. Thus Paul explained in detail the error into which Peter fell unintentionally, so that all might know the seriousness of its meaning.

But St. Peter was not angry; rather, he submitted himself to the rebuke for the sake of the truth of the Gospel, and he said in his second epistle, "Even as our beloved brother Paul" (2 Pet 3:15). Although Peter had supported Paul at the council of Jerusalem in accepting the Gentiles, Paul did not hesitate here to declare the truth and rebuke Peter openly for the salvation of souls. This verse and those after it are either addressed to Peter, or Paul has begun his speech to the Galatians.

entries.section: (4) Justification by Christ and not by the works of the Law

paragraphs.text: I through the law am dead: that is, the Law condemned me and carried out the sentence of death on me because I did not keep it. To the law: since I have believed in Christ, I have been freed from the Law and have become dead to it and from it, that is, not bound by it but by the perfect commandments of Christ.

Christ died for us and bore our sins in our place, and gave us His life and His freedom that we may live forever, since we were baptized with Him in the likeness of His death and rose with Him, freed from the ritual Law.

entries.section: (4) Justification by Christ and not by the works of the Law

paragraphs.text: I am crucified with Christ: Paul feels, as a believer in Christ, that by faith he has been united with the crucified Christ, who fulfilled the Law and paid the debt of sin on the cross by His death. Consequently every believer who is crucified with Christ dies to the Law, and the Law no longer has authority over him.
Nevertheless I live: Christ by His resurrection grants me life after the death that had been decreed against me because of sin.
Yet not I: not by my own thought and capacities, or my passions and desires.

Christ liveth in me: this new life is a gift from Christ, so I live it for Him, and all my thoughts, my words and my actions are for Christ. He is the One who moves me, and He is the One who dwells and works in me, and He is my life. Paul declares, on behalf of every believer in Christ, that his life is founded on faith in Christ, who died out of love for us, so that he lives for Him.

entries.section: (4) Justification by Christ and not by the works of the Law

paragraphs.text: Paul makes clear the conclusion of his speech with Peter, or with the Galatians: that the Law does not justify man, otherwise why was there any need for Christ to die? Consequently, clinging to the Law after faith in Christ nullifies this faith and the justification that results from it. Of course Paul did not nullify it, but declares that there is no need to cling to the Law after faith in Christ, whether for Christians of Jewish origin or, all the more, for Christians of Gentile origin, who do not need the Law.

May you crucify all evil desires with Christ and die to them so that you may live for Him, and then you will use everything and nothing will enslave you. And as you enjoy the prayers and the readings and are united with Him in the sacrament of Holy Communion, you will feel His presence with you, and even see Him in all the creation around you.
Justification by faith and not by the Law

entries.section: (1) Rebuking the Galatians for clinging to the works of the Law

paragraphs.text: Foolish: Paul rebukes the Galatians for their great ignorance in believing that the Law is the cause of their salvation, so that they clung to it after they were baptized. Paul does not break the commandment by saying "foolish", because he is their teacher and their father, responsible for them, and he rebukes them over the most important matter in their lives, which is their salvation, but he kept his peace and was not angry.
Bewitched you: that is, enchanted you, from the incantation used in sorcery; it means that he changed you completely, to this degree, away from the right faith.
Obey: submit and be obedient.
The truth: the faith, because Christ alone is the Savior and not the works of the Law.
Jesus Christ hath been evidently set forth, crucified among you: in the ancient Greek original in which the Holy Bible was written, it means picturing the crucified Christ in the mind.
The Apostle rebukes the Galatians for leaving faith in Christ the Savior and returning to reliance on the Law as a source of salvation.

entries.section: (1) Rebuking the Galatians for clinging to the works of the Law

paragraphs.text: The hearing of faith: the preaching and proclaiming of Christ the Savior that Paul delivered among them. Paul asks the Galatians, in astonishment, about the cause of the blessings in which they live, which is the work of the Holy Spirit in them with all His gifts and fruits: is it the works of the Law or their faith in Christ the Savior? Of course the answer is that the Holy Spirit and all His gifts are grace which they receive by faith.

entries.section: (1) Rebuking the Galatians for clinging to the works of the Law

paragraphs.text: Man is supposed to grow spiritually, but they began with faith and went back to the fleshly ordinances of the Law such as circumcision.

entries.section: (1) Rebuking the Galatians for clinging to the works of the Law

paragraphs.text: Your endurance of sufferings and persecutions for the sake of Christ was not in vain; what is in vain is the attempt to reach perfection by the works of the Law.

entries.section: (1) Rebuking the Galatians for clinging to the works of the Law

paragraphs.text: Paul repeats the question so that they may examine themselves: did they attain these gifts and powers because of their commitment to the Law or by the power of faith? ... Paul was always urging steadfastness in faith: "Now the just shall live by faith: but if any man draw back, my soul shall have no pleasure in him" (Heb 10:38), "work out your own salvation with fear and trembling" (Phil 2:12). Perhaps this passage answers those who say that a believer cannot fall away. For these fell away after they had believed, because they listened to the false teachers.

Let us constantly examine ourselves: is our spiritual life advancing or declining?! If we notice a decline, we look for the cause, which may be negligence toward a certain sin or shortcoming in our prayers and readings, and repentance and confession bring us back again to the way of the Kingdom.

entries.section: (2) Abraham, the example of justification by faith

paragraphs.text: The Apostle Paul presents proofs from Scripture, taking Abraham, the father of the Jewish people, as an example that justification is by faith and not by the works of the Law. For Abraham believed, and his faith was counted as righteousness, and this was before the Law of Moses and before circumcision (Gen 15:6).

entries.section: (2) Abraham, the example of justification by faith

paragraphs.text: The Apostle affirms that belonging to Abraham is according to the active faith of Abraham and not according to physical descent, and therefore the Lord Christ said to them, "If ye were Abraham's children, ye would do the works of Abraham" (Jn 8:39). And because God had foreseen that the Gentiles would believe in Christ, He promised Abraham, "in thy seed (Christ) shall all the nations of the earth be blessed" (Gen 26:4). So whoever walks in the way of Abraham in faith receives the promise of blessing. Abraham's faith was practical, for he left everything and obeyed and offered his only son Isaac, so God said to him, "By myself have I sworn, saith the LORD, for because thou hast done this thing, and hast not withheld thy son, thine only son: That in blessing I will bless thee, and in multiplying I will multiply thy seed as the stars of the heaven, and as the sand which is upon the sea shore" (Gen 22:16, 17). So the work here is the work of grace in man's life as a result of living faith, and there is no place for the Law in God's promise to Abraham.

Let us have practical faith in our lives, so that we bring God into all our works and trust in His supporting power, and are not troubled by tribulations, for He is able to bring us through them and we come out stronger.

entries.section: (3) A comparison between the Law and faith

paragraphs.text: Whoever lives by the Law will not be able to fulfill everything in it, and so he becomes deficient and cursed, because he sinned by not fulfilling the Law. The book of Deuteronomy affirms this (Deut 27:26), and this verse is cited here to declare the necessity of fulfilling the whole Law, or else man becomes cursed.

entries.section: (3) A comparison between the Law and faith

paragraphs.text: Justification, then, will not be by the Law, which curses everyone who falls short in one point of it, but by faith, as the prophet Habakkuk mentions in his prophecy (Hab 2:4).

entries.section: (3) A comparison between the Law and faith

paragraphs.text: The difference between faith and the works of the Law is clear. The latter does not justify the one who neglects them, and there is no one who can live by all the demands of the Law, so life and justification are by faith, while the Law prepared the way for faith in Christ.

entries.section: (3) A comparison between the Law and faith

paragraphs.text: Christ fulfilled the Law for us, for He alone was able to do so, and He was crucified for us. Crucifixion is the sign of shame and of the curse, that is, Christ the Righteous became a curse for us in order to remove from us the curse and the need to fulfill the Law. He fulfilled it for us so that we might believe in Him and receive justification, and no longer need to fulfill the works of the Law.

entries.section: (3) A comparison between the Law and faith

paragraphs.text: Thus it appears that justification is by faith and not by the works of the Law. Not only the Jews who believe, but the Gentiles also, so that all receive justification in Christ and the work of the Holy Spirit with all His gifts and fruits overflows upon them.

If salvation is available to us when we believe in Christ, let us no longer rely on our own ideas or on our abilities apart from God, but trust in Christ and rely on Him in everything, to open the way for the work of the Holy Spirit in us.

entries.section: (4) The Law does not annul the promises

paragraphs.text: Brethren: because they are believers and members of the one body of Christ.
After the manner of men: that is, by human reasoning.
Confirmed: made firm.
It is well known that any promise made by any man remains firm, and no one can take anything from it or add anything to it. How much more, then, if the promise is from God, it remains firm.

entries.section: (4) The Law does not annul the promises

paragraphs.text: The divine promises were made to Abraham, and of course they remain firm and no one can break them. God promised Abraham and said "to thy seed" and not "to seeds". So what is meant is one person and not a group, and this person is Christ, who came from the seed of Abraham and offers salvation to the whole world, so that the whole world that believes in Him is blessed in Him.

entries.section: (4) The Law does not annul the promises

paragraphs.text: Disannul: abolish.

Paul declares that the Law, which was given to Moses about 430 years after God's promise to Abraham, cannot abolish God's promises. The promises are salvation by Christ the Redeemer, so the Law cannot abolish them and be a substitute for them in man's salvation; rather, the Law is merely the preparer of the way for faith in Christ.

entries.section: (4) The Law does not annul the promises

paragraphs.text: The inheritance of salvation is not by the Law but by God's promise which He gave to Abraham and which is fulfilled in Christ. If salvation were by the Law, then it would not be by God's promise to Abraham, that is, salvation would not be by Christ. Of course the Jews do not accept the abolition of the divine promise to Abraham, which is fulfilled only in Christ. So salvation and justification are by Christ and not by the Law, because the inheritance by the Law is considered a wage for the one who fulfills it, whereas the inheritance by the divine promise is a free gift, and these two are opposites. So Paul affirms that God gave the inheritance to Abraham by promise and not by the works of the Law, and this promise is fulfilled through salvation in Christ, while the Law made known to us sin and its penalty, that is, it was a preparation for Christ, in whom we believe, so that He saves us from its penalty and we live with Him and in Him the new life.

entries.section: (4) The purpose of the Law

paragraphs.text: Added: put in addition.
Transgressions: the many sins into which man fell after God's promise to Abraham.
The seed: Christ.
Angels: those who gave Moses the Law.
Mediator: Moses.

The Apostle Paul poses a question and answers it: since the Law did not justify us, why did God give it after His promise to Abraham? The answer is that people did not walk according to the faith of our father Abraham, so God laid down for them the statutes of the Law like a bridle that restrains them so that they do not slip into evil, and to lead them in carrying out the commandment, so He made known to them sin and its penalty. But until when?.. Until Christ comes, and when He comes the mission of the Law ends. And the Apostle Paul declares that the Law, according to the inherited Jewish tradition, was given by God to Moses by means of angels, to deliver it and explain it to Moses, as St. Stephen indicated: "Who have received the law by the disposition of angels, and have not kept it" (Acts 7:53).

entries.section: (4) The purpose of the Law

paragraphs.text: Is not a mediator of one: mediation is always between two, and the Law is a mediator between two, who are God and man.
But God is one: He is the One who gave the promise as a free gift without the intervention of man, and this promise is fulfilled in Christ the Savior. So salvation is by Christ and not by the Law.

The mediator is between two parties, and Moses himself can be considered a mediator who carried God's Law to the people. The Law did not depend only on the giver of the commandment but also on man's keeping of the Law, because it is a covenant between two, but he failed.

There is no contradiction between this verse and the speaking of Christ as the mediator for reconciling man with God (1 Tim 2:5), because Christ, since the Law failed in its mediation between God and man, came incarnate and as the Redeemer of man to fulfill the divine promise given to Abraham.

entries.section: (4) The purpose of the Law

paragraphs.text: Paul strongly denies that the Law which God gave is against His promises, because the Law, as we mentioned, reveals sin and its penalty, that is, it alerts man to it so that he rejects it. But man alone is unable to repent and be rid of sin, and he needs Christ the Savior, who rescues him and gives him life.
Therefore the Law is unable to give man the new life, because it does not save him from sin and does not justify him.

entries.section: (4) The purpose of the Law

paragraphs.text: The scripture: the books of the Holy Bible, especially the legislation, that is, the Law.

Concluded: it showed the weakness of all people and their deserving of judgment and eternal death because of their sins. The Law condemned all people and sentenced them to death because of their sins, their transgressions of it and their shortcomings, and by this it prepared for the work of Christ, who saves man from the prison of sin and gives him new life (1 Pet 3:19).

entries.section: (4) The purpose of the Law

paragraphs.text: Paul makes clear that before the Incarnation of Christ the people of God were under the guard of the Law, which alerted them to sin so that they tried to keep away from it, and consequently they were better than the pagans who made light of sin. So the people of God differed in their character and customs from the rest of the peoples, since the Law kept them and shut them in so that they would not go astray by treating sin as permissible. But they were unable to fulfill the whole Law, so they were sentenced to death and shut up in the prison of sin until Christ came and freed them from it by His redemption. So the Law kept the people of God until, in the fullness of time, faith in Christ the Savior would be revealed.

entries.section: (4) The purpose of the Law

paragraphs.text: The Apostle Paul shows the work of the Law not only in keeping the people of God but also in disciplining them. As a tutor or instructor, it showed the wrongs so that people would keep away from them, but it did not save them, so they understood truth from falsehood and felt their need for the salvation that was accomplished by Christ.

entries.section: (4) The purpose of the Law

paragraphs.text: Therefore, after faith in Christ, who gives us the ability to leave sin and moves us to the new, pure life, we do not need the Law, whose work ended with the coming of Christ.

Accept warning and rebuke from others and take refuge in God, who gives you by the Holy Spirit repentance and new life in His Church. And be submissive to the work of the Holy Spirit in you, who always guides you to life with God.

entries.section: (6) Faith and sonship in Christ

paragraphs.text: The Apostle Paul declares that all who believe in Christ have become sons of God and not slaves, because they were born again in Baptism and so became sons of God and put on a new nature which Christ the Savior gave them, and became members united with the body of Christ, that is, the Church. In faith all human distinctions have ended, such as a man's being Jewish by origin or Greek, that is, a Gentile who is not a Jew, and He also ended the difference between slaves and free, since He raised all to the rank of sonship to God by Baptism. Likewise the ancient peoples, and some religions until now, regarded woman as lower than man, but he declared that male and female have become in one standing, that is, sons of God by Baptism, and have put on Christ, that is, the new nature. So all Christians are one before God, regardless of differences of origin, social standing, sex or any other differences.

entries.section: (6) Faith and sonship in Christ

paragraphs.text: Paul reaches the final conclusion, which is that faith in Christ is the fulfillment of God's promises to Abraham, so the believers become children of Abraham and heirs of the Kingdom. This spiritual sonship by faith and Baptism is the true sonship, and not the physical sonship that the Jews imagined for themselves and boasted of.

Contemplate the grace you enjoy, which you received by Baptism, which is the new nature inclined to become like God. And if by Baptism you have put on Christ, do not act except according to His will, so that you are a living image of Him that draws people to Him and does not cause them to stumble. Thus you will be walking with steady steps on the way of the Kingdom. Sons and heirs

entries.section: (1) From minor to heir

paragraphs.text: The heir: signifies the believers in the Old Testament.

Tutors (guardians): the guardian is the one who, by law, has charge of the minor child so that he does not reach out for the inheritance before the age of maturity. The guardian here signifies the Law.

Governors (stewards): the steward is the one appointed by the guardian to look after the child's affairs in his living, health and education, and here he signifies the ordinances of the Law and its rulings.
The time appointed: the time of the Incarnation of Christ and His redemption.
The elements of the world: that is, the material ordinances of the Law such as purifications and washings.

The believers in the Old Testament were subject to the commandments of the Law and its material rulings, and strove by them to fulfill it, but they failed and were unable to be freed from the yoke of bondage to sin so as to enjoy their rights as sons. So they were in the condition of slaves, awaiting the Messiah the Savior to set them free, like minor children for whom the time has not come to act freely in their inheritance, that is, their sonship to God which they receive in the Christian life.
God has given us a very special boldness toward Him so that we may enjoy His fatherhood and speak to Him about our life, our circumstances and our hopes. Do we use it?

entries.section: (1) From minor to heir

paragraphs.text: The fulness of the time: the time of the Incarnation of Christ and His redemption.
A woman: the Virgin Mary.
Under the law: that is, He was born a Jew subject to the Law.

The eternal Son became incarnate of the Virgin to take our human nature, and was born as a Jew to fulfill the Law on behalf of man, who was unable to fulfill it, and then to die without any sin that He had committed, in order to take away our sins and redeem all people who are unable to fulfill the Law. Since He fulfilled it for us and died for our redemption, He gave us sonship to Him, so we became sons by adoption. This, of course, is different from the Son's sonship in essence from eternity with the Father.

He was born of a woman and took our human nature so that He could redeem mankind, and because He is God, the Infinite, His sacrifice is able to forgive all the sins of the world, which are infinite and directed against the infinite God.

entries.section: (1) From minor to heir

paragraphs.text: The Spirit of his Son: the Holy Spirit.
Abba: "father" in Syriac, which means "Papa."
Father: "father" in Greek.

Since in the New Testament we receive sonship to God through Baptism, we become qualified for the work of the Holy Spirit of God in us, who gives us the boldness of sonship and teaches us how to pray and feel God's fatherhood, so that we call Him "Papa, Father." Paul mentioned it in both languages to confirm the meaning of sonship.

entries.section: (1) From minor to heir

paragraphs.text: Thus the believer moves from the bondage of sin, which the Law reveals, to sonship to God by faith and Baptism, and by this sonship the Kingdom of Heaven awaits him as a reward from Christ, if he stays firm in his sonship to God throughout his life.

Your sonship to God opens wide horizons for you in your relationship with Him. It gives you reassurance, a striving to become like Him, and an inclination to be with Him, so that you experience Him not only in prayers and readings and in union in the sacrament of the Eucharist, but also behold Him and feel Him with you in all your steps, until you enjoy being with Him forever in heaven.

entries.section: (2) Returning to the Law after faith

paragraphs.text: Which by nature are no gods: that is, the idols.
Are known of God: that is, God loved you, accepted you and redeemed you.
Weak elements: the fleshly commandments of the Law such as circumcision.
Beggarly: that is, empty of grace, relying on failing human effort.

Paul reminds the Galatians that they were far from God and worshiped idols, but they believed in Christ and He accepted them and saved them from their sins. How then do they return to reliance on the Law, which does not save its followers, because there is no grace of God in it, but it is merely a revealing of sin and its hideousness?

Thank God for His care for you and for the salvation offered to you on the altar every day as true Body and Blood, and ask His help in all your steps, and He will support you and you will succeed in all your works.

entries.section: (2) Returning to the Law after faith

paragraphs.text: Days, and months, and times, and years: the times that the Law set for worship and feasts.
Bestowed upon you labour: I preached to you.

The Apostle Paul is astonished at the Galatians' clinging to the Law as the foundation of their salvation, so that he declares his fear for them, that they did not understand his message about Christ and laid a foundation for salvation other than His blood shed for them. Of course this is different from the Church's concern for feasts and fasts, because they are an expression of love and spiritual remembrances resulting from faith in Christ and not a foundation for obtaining salvation. They are necessary expressions for every true believer who loves Christ, so that he does not forget Him amid the preoccupations of life.

entries.section: (3) Reminding the Galatians of their first love

paragraphs.text: Be as I am: in my faith in the blood of Christ the Savior alone.
For I am as ye are: I do not cling to the distinction and rights of the Jews but live as one of the Gentiles.
Ye have not injured me at all: you were kind in your treatment of me when I visited you, and you honored me.

Paul spoke with kindness and humility to the Galatians, and entreats them to believe as he does that salvation is by the blood of Christ alone and not by the Law, because their sonship to him and their love lead them to follow his example. His fatherhood also made him deal with them as one of them, and he did not boast of his advantages as a Jew from the people of God and better than the pagan Gentiles. Then he reminds them of their kindness in dealing with him when he visited them and preached to them, and of their first love for him, and calls them to return to their sonship to him and not to follow the false teachings of the teachers of Jewish origin who turn against him and his teachings.

entries.section: (3) Reminding the Galatians of their first love

paragraphs.text: Infirmity of the flesh: Paul's bodily weakness, which was most likely the weakness of his eyesight and sores on his body that he used to bind with pieces of cloth.
At the first: that is, his first visit to Galatia.
My temptation: my illnesses.
As an angel of God: you honored me as an angel sent from God.

Paul testifies that he suffered from illnesses in his body when he visited and preached in Galatia, and that the Galatians were not troubled by his bodily weakness nor did they despise him, but on the contrary they felt that he was like an angel whom God had sent to them and an image of Christ, for they saw Christ in him, so they honored him greatly.

entries.section: (3) Reminding the Galatians of their first love

paragraphs.text: The blessedness ye spake of: the praise you received from others because of your strong love for me.

Paul asks about the Galatians' strong love for him, for which everyone praises them: where has it gone, and how did they turn against him because he rebuked them for believing that the Law is a condition for receiving salvation, as the false teachers claimed? At the same time he encourages them by testifying to their intense love for him, and that they would have wished, if possible, to pluck out their eyes and give them to him so that he could see with them. It is understood that his temptation was the weakness of his eyesight, as proved by the fact that he used to dictate his epistles to one of his disciples, as is mentioned at the end of each epistle. This epistle, however, he wrote himself, but in large letters (ch. 6:11). This may support the opinion of some who say that this epistle was written early, before the other epistles, when his sight was better than afterward.

entries.section: (3) Reminding the Galatians of their first love

paragraphs.text: Because I tell you the truth: I declared that your acceptance of the teaching of the false teachers separates you from Christ and you return to Judaism.
Paul is astonished at the change in the Galatians from intense love for him to enmity toward him, because he was frank with them and declared to them their error in accepting the false teachers.

entries.section: (3) Reminding the Galatians of their first love

paragraphs.text: They zealously affect you: the false teachers show their love for the Galatians so that they follow them in their mistaken teachings.
Exclude you: draw you away from true faith in Christ.
Ye might affect them: you love them and become attached to their differing teachings.

Paul warns the Galatians of the deceit of the false teachers in their self-serving love for them, in order to gain followers of their mistaken ideas. This love is evil and draws them away from the truth, so that they become attached to these teachers and follow them in their deviations.

entries.section: (3) Reminding the Galatians of their first love

paragraphs.text: Paul praises the people's love for their teachers and their obedience to them, but in sound and good teachings and not false teachings. The Galatians loved Paul and obeyed his message when he visited them, so would that they remain firm in this faith in Christ and in their love for him.

entries.section: (3) Reminding the Galatians of their first love

paragraphs.text: Paul speaks in a spirit of fatherhood toward the Galatians and likens himself to the mother who suffers the pains of childbirth (labor). He bears their fickleness and tries to bring them back to sound faith so that he may bring them forth as children of Christ and a true image of Him.

entries.section: (3) Reminding the Galatians of their first love

paragraphs.text: To change my voice: to speak with kindness and encouragement instead of the rebuke that I wrote in this epistle.

I stand in doubt of you: I do not know whether you have been convinced by the proofs I have given, or whether it is better to rebuke you firmly or encourage you gently so that you return to the faith safe.

Paul wishes to visit Galatia to know how its people respond to his message, and to show his fatherhood with words of tenderness and encouragement in order to win them for Christ. He is ready to rebuke them, convince them and encourage them, that is, to use every way to bring them back to their first faith in Christ.

Praise the behavior of those around you so that you win their love and encourage them to accept your guidance that binds them to Christ, because if they are at ease with you and love you they will obey your teachings and be attached to the Church.

entries.section: (4) A comparison between the seed of Sarah and of Hagar

paragraphs.text: The law: the five books of Moses.

St. Paul says to the Galatians: If you do not want to listen to the Gospel, then go back to our father Abraham, in whom the Jews boast as their greatest father. He compares at length Hagar the bondwoman, whose name means Sinai, who emigrated to the wilderness of Sinai, and whose offspring was a symbol of the bondage under the Law and the heirs of the earthly Jerusalem, and Sarah the free woman, whose name means princess and mother of many, and whose offspring is a symbol of the freedom that is in Christ and the heirs of the heavenly Jerusalem. Ishmael is the son of the flesh according to fleshly counsel, and Hagar represents the covenant of the Law which God gave to the children of Israel on Mount Sinai in the Arabian desert, which is the land of Hagar's descendants. All her children were born into bondage, and the covenant was conditional on obedience: "Now therefore, if ye will obey my voice indeed, and keep my covenant, then ye shall be a peculiar treasure unto me" (Ex 19:5). The Jews used to boast that they were children of Abraham and had never been in bondage to anyone, so the Apostle Paul told them that everyone who returns to be enslaved to the Law is a son of Hagar and a son of the earthly Jerusalem, and is a captive to the rulings and ordinances of the Law, and remains a slave who does not inherit.

entries.section: (4) A comparison between the seed of Sarah and of Hagar

paragraphs.text: Paul declares that he is using the wives of Abraham, Hagar and Sarah, as a representation and symbol of those who are subject to the Law, that is, the Jews, and of those who enjoy faith, that is, the Christians. He distinguishes between them by saying "two covenants": the first, which Hagar signifies, is the one made on Mount Sinai, because the meaning of the word Hagar is Sinai, as the ancient Arabs called it, and on this mountain Moses received the Law to which the Jews cling, and whose capital in the time of the Apostle Paul was Jerusalem. Paul affirms that the Jews are enslaved to the Law, which reveals only the faults of man, and have not yet received the freedom of the children of God through their Christian faith.

entries.section: (4) A comparison between the seed of Sarah and of Hagar

paragraphs.text: Jerusalem which is above: he means the Church of the New Testament, the Christian Church, which is higher and loftier than the Law, that is, the earthly Jerusalem, and the goal of the Christian Church is the heavenly Jerusalem. The mother of us all: the Christian Church is the mother of all believers, and it is signified by Sarah, who is the mother of all believers through her son Isaac.

Free: Sarah is the free lady and not a bondwoman, and her children are the believers in Christ, whom He freed from the death of sin and the bondage of the Law, which sentences them to death because they are sinners, since Christ accomplished redemption by His death on their behalf and gave them the new, free life in Him.
The Apostle makes clear that the Church, the mother of all believers, is free from the chains of the Law.

entries.section: (4) A comparison between the seed of Sarah and of Hagar

paragraphs.text: Thou barren .. thou that travailest not: he means Sarah, who signifies the Gentiles far from the faith, who had no fruit of life with God.
The children of the desolate: the children of Sarah by faith, that is, the Gentiles.
Her which hath an husband: the children of Hagar, by whom he means the Jews enslaved to the Law, because Hagar, as we mentioned, signifies Mount Sinai on which Moses received the Law.
Paul cites the prophet Isaiah (Isa 54:1), who speaks about Jerusalem forsaken in the days of the captivity, but it would be rebuilt and its sons would return from the captivity.

The same prophecy is about the Gentiles far from God, who will believe in the Christian Church and become the majority in it. So Isaiah says, "Rejoice, thou barren" who was formerly barren (Sarah), which signifies the Church of the Gentiles, while she "which hath an husband" signifies the Jews.

entries.section: (4) A comparison between the seed of Sarah and of Hagar

paragraphs.text: As Isaac was: like.

We, as Christians, are children of promise, born by faith from the font of Baptism, which is the womb of the Church our mother, born from above by our faith in God's promise of redemption, and we return to our free mother, the heavenly Jerusalem, because everyone who believed and acted by the faith of Abraham and Sarah became a son of Abraham, as Isaac was, the son of promise.

entries.section: (4) A comparison between the seed of Sarah and of Hagar

paragraphs.text: Born after the flesh: he is Ishmael, who signifies the Jews who live by the fleshly ordinances of the Law.

After the Spirit: he is Isaac, who signifies the Christian Church, most of which is of Gentile origin. At the weaning of Isaac his parents made a feast, and Sarah saw the son of the bondwoman mocking, and it is said that he was aiming his arrows at Isaac, threatening to kill him as a way of frightening him (Gen 21:9). This is an example of the Jews' persecution of the Christians.

entries.section: (4) A comparison between the seed of Sarah and of Hagar

paragraphs.text: Sarah said to Abraham, cast out the bondwoman, for the son of the bondwoman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman (Gen 21:10), and the Lord said to him, listen to all that Sarah has said to you. For the inheritance is only for the sons born from above: "Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God" (Jn 3:3). It means that there can be no agreement between the Jews who insist that the Law is a condition for salvation and the true believers who know that salvation is by the blood of Christ alone. Therefore the false teachers, that is, the Christians of Jewish origin who try to bring Christianity back to Judaism by submitting to the Law, have no share in the Church.

entries.section: (4) A comparison between the seed of Sarah and of Hagar

paragraphs.text: In conclusion, the Apostle Paul sums up the position of the believers in the Christian Church: they are the children of Sarah the free woman, that is, the children of faith in Christ, who frees them from the bondage of sin, and not the children of the bondwoman Hagar, that is, those subject to the Law with its ordinances, which reveal man's weakness and do not save him. So he rejects clinging to the Law after faith in Christ.

Let us hold fast to the work of grace in our lives and struggle by it to overcome the bad habits that dominate us, confident of God's power however repeated or hard our sins may be, and our confidence in the new life that God has given us urges us to quick repentance, to holding fast to the Church and to doing good. Christian freedom

entries.section: (1) Stand fast in freedom

paragraphs.text: Stand fast therefore: the "therefore" completes the discourse with which the previous chapter ended, that the believers are children of Sarah the free woman and not children of bondage from the bondwoman. The word indicates their wavering. Freedom was given to them as a gift, and all that is required of them is to stand fast in it, for the slave does not abide in the house forever, but the son abides and inherits.

Be not entangled: do not turn aside from the upright faith and enslave yourselves to the ordinances and works of the Law. For this reason we find that worship in Christianity is in spirit and in truth. Fasts and prayers were established not to enslave man but to serve him, and through them he offers sacrifices of thanksgiving and praise to God with the love of sons and not the fear of slaves.

I Paul say unto you: that is, I am confident of what I say, that whoever clings to circumcision does not trust in the grace found in the blood of Christ the Savior alone, and consequently, by his unbelief, will not benefit from the salvation of Christ.
The Apostle calls them to be freed from the bondage of the Law and circumcision so that they may live with God in the Church in the freedom of sons.

entries.section: (1) Stand fast in freedom

paragraphs.text: Whoever among them commits himself to circumcision will be bound to keep the whole Law, because circumcision is linked with purification, offering sacrifices and keeping the Jewish ceremonies. Clinging to circumcision means returning from Christianity to Judaism and committing oneself to all its obligations, and a rejection of Christ. Consequently he warns the Galatians, who are Gentiles and believed in Christ, not to be circumcised as the false teachers, who are Jews converted to Christianity, call them to do.

entries.section: (1) Stand fast in freedom

paragraphs.text: Christ is become of no effect unto you: that is, you have made the work of Christ void in you.

Ye are fallen from grace: if man enslaves himself to the ordinances of the Law, grace forsakes him and he falls from eternal life, because grace is what keeps him standing in righteousness and holiness. Paul declares that whoever clings to circumcision and the Law will lose the salvation of Christ and the work of His grace in him.

Do not lose the work of God's grace in you by relying on material things or relationships, or by fearing the envy or power of people. On the contrary, persevere in your prayers even if the solution to your problems is delayed, confident of God's care and power.

entries.section: (2) Faith that works

paragraphs.text: By the Holy Spirit, whom we received by faith and who dwelt in us in Baptism, we have the hope of righteousness, of salvation to the end at the Second Coming. For in Jesus Christ neither circumcision nor separation avails anything, but faith which worketh by love. What is required is faith and not circumcision and the Law, but not theoretical faith; rather, faith that shows itself in works of love and mercy toward others.

entries.section: (2) Faith that works

paragraphs.text: Ye did run: it conveys activity and alertness.
Did hinder you: that is, obstructed you, so that you do not obey God who called you and turn aside from the way of truth by submitting to these deceivers, whose obedience is not from God.

A little leaven: what is meant is committing oneself to circumcision, which will lead them to complete Judaizing. The Apostle asks them what made them turn aside from the way of truth after they had been advancing on the way of grace. For a small error, if they do not quickly remedy it, will become a great danger.

Do not be lenient with a small sin lest it lead you to a greater one, because Satan most often draws you gradually into evil. So be careful and examine yourself every day in repentance together with your prayer, and take care to disclose all your sins and their causes in the sacrament of confession.

entries.section: (2) Faith that works

paragraphs.text: I have confidence in you through the Lord: he praises them and encourages them to correct their error, but our confidence must be in our God and not in ourselves.
That ye will be none otherwise minded: the Jews spread the word that the Apostle Paul preaches circumcision because he is a circumcised Jew and he allowed the circumcision of Timothy.
Shall bear his judgment: these deceivers have placed themselves under judgment because they are not in Christ.
Whosoever he be: whatever his position or fame.
Were even cut off: their separation from the teaching and from association with the believers in the Church.

After praising the Galatians, Paul denies that he has preached circumcision, and says, if I preach circumcision, why am I still persecuted by the Jews?..!! As for me, I preach only the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, which to the Jews is a stumbling block because it makes everyone equal, Jews and Gentiles, but the Jews want distinction. Would that these were cut off from the Church.

entries.section: (3) Freedom in the Christian understanding

paragraphs.text: The Son has set us free, and we have become truly free from the bondage of sin by the power of God's grace, and from the Law of Moses by the power of the death of Christ for us. So do not use freedom to give free rein to the lusts of the flesh, but so that you may rise in spirit to a loftier thought and a higher level. For freedom in Christianity makes the believer enslave himself, by himself, to the service of others in love, and the thief no longer steals but labors and works to help the needy. So we are governed by the law of love.

entries.section: (3) Freedom in the Christian understanding

paragraphs.text: Bite and devour: you harm and wound one another as an animal pounces on its prey to tear it and eat it.

If the sum of the Law is love for others, why do you walk in the opposite way, by condemning and exploiting one another? And by continuing these offenses and transgressions you destroy yourselves and draw away from God. If you bite and devour one another, where are you then from the law of love, and will circumcision benefit you?!

The goal of Christianity is love, which, as it grows toward God, appears in our dealings with others. And Satan tries to restrain our love with the preoccupations of sin and the cares of the world. When we are freed from them by repentance, we are released in love toward everyone. The proof of your freedom is the growth of your love toward others and your readiness to give even to the one who wrongs you.

entries.section: (4) Walk in the Spirit

paragraphs.text: Walk in the Spirit: submission to the Holy Spirit.
The Apostle Paul calls us to the spiritual walk and not to be led away after evil fleshly lusts.

entries.section: (4) Walk in the Spirit

paragraphs.text: The flesh: he means the evil fleshly lusts.
The Spirit: he means man's spirit submitted to the Holy Spirit.

The flesh, inclined to lusts, opposes the spiritual desires that his spirit seeks, and the spirit strives to bring man to life with God, but it is hindered by the flesh's attachment to lusts, so that when man desires with his spirit a pure relationship with God and people, his lustful flesh draws him by his laxity toward it, and he does the opposite of what he wants by the Spirit.

entries.section: (4) Walk in the Spirit

paragraphs.text: Those who are led by the Holy Spirit have every evil desire and lust quenched in them, and consequently they do not need the restraints of the Law, as often as they practice the means of grace that increase the work of the Holy Spirit in them, such as Communion, repentance, prayer and reading the Holy Bible; they have experienced the new life with Christ.

entries.section: (5) The works of the flesh and the works of the Spirit

paragraphs.text: The works of the flesh, which refused to be led by the Holy Spirit, produce corruption, but if man submits his flesh to the leadership of the Holy Spirit, his life bears virtues by the work of the Holy Spirit. The Apostle Paul gave samples of sins, seventeen sins, which are divided into three categories:

1- Six works for the gratification of the lusts of the flesh (adultery - uncleanness - lasciviousness - fornication): the use of sexual instincts for forbidden pleasure. Lasciviousness: the adultery of the married.
Uncleanness - fornication: trafficking in sex.
Drunkenness: excess in drinking wine.
Revellings: a kind of rowdiness and wrath resulting from drunkenness.
2- Two works against God:
Idolatry: not only by bowing down to idols, but the love of money is also considered a kind of idolatry (Col 3:5). Witchcraft: directly connected with Satan.
3- Nine works against others:
Hatred: hatred of another or stirring up enmities among people.
Variance: detesting another and shunning him.
Emulations: resentment of another's distinction over me, and I may seek to harm him.
Wrath: an outburst of anger and intense rage.
Strife: a faction that leads to division and to harming others.
Seditions: divisions.
Heresies: heresy and deviant teachings.
Envyings: vindictiveness toward others and a grudge that cannot bear their success.
Murders: ending a life, or a moral murder by severe insult.
And whoever does such sins shall not inherit the kingdom of God.

entries.section: (5) The works of the flesh and the works of the Spirit

paragraphs.text: He did not say fruits but the fruit of the Spirit, because they all come from one tree planted by the streams of the waters of the Holy Spirit. He mentions nine fruits of it, divided into three categories: 1) a hidden category that expresses the believer's state from within:

Love: the sign of being born from above: "We know that we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren" (1 Jn 3:14). Joy: a joy that no one can take from the believer's heart and that is not affected by surrounding circumstances. Peace: the peace of God which passes all understanding fills the heart in the severest tribulations.
2) A category that appears in the believer's relationship with others.
Longsuffering: by grace he acquires a superior ability to be patient and to bear the offenses of others, remembering our Lord's patience with him for his salvation.
Gentleness: dealing with meekness, compassion, kindness and forgiveness instead of harshness and roughness. Goodness: doing virtue in every situation with generosity and liberality.
3) A personal category:

Faith: believing in things unseen with complete trust in God, relying on Him and abiding in Him. Meekness: accepting offense from others with a broad heart like the Lord Christ, "learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart" (Mt 11:29), with quietness of voice and conduct.
Temperance: controlling the lusts of the flesh and sanctifying the senses and feelings to God.
Against such there is no law: God's law agrees with the preceding fruits, and if it says otherwise, it is not a law from God.

entries.section: (5) The works of the flesh and the works of the Spirit

paragraphs.text: They that are Christ's: they are those who accepted Him as Lord, Redeemer and Savior and believed in Him.
The believers in Christ are His own, who followed Him and have put to death the lusts of the flesh by grace and by the power of the Holy Spirit.

entries.section: (5) The works of the flesh and the works of the Spirit

paragraphs.text: If we live in the Spirit, that is, by the power of the Holy Spirit, it is fitting for us to walk according to the principles of the Spirit and to side with His leadership.

entries.section: (5) The works of the flesh and the works of the Spirit

paragraphs.text: Whoever walks in the Spirit is not conceited, that is, proud, because the sin of pride leads to anger and selfishness; man wants everything for himself and envies others if they obtain something that he does not have.

As Christ left everything for your sake on the cross, would that you leave something of your comfort and material desires for His sake, that is, that you control your passions, repent of your sins, and give yourself an opportunity for prayer and for hearing His voice in the Holy Bible.
Compassion for sinners - giving to the teachers

entries.section: (1) Compassion for sinners

paragraphs.text: Overtaken: that is, Satan overcame him and made him fall.
A man: to show human weakness.
Fault: that is, his feet slipped and he fell into sin.

The Apostle Paul began his epistle with rebuke, saying "O foolish", and ends it with gentleness, "brethren", in order to win everyone to Christ. For Christianity did not lay down ordinances and rulings but principles that lift the believers to what is higher than the law. So they, as spiritual people, if a man among them falls into a fault, must restore him and not judge him, that is, bring him back from his error in a spirit of meekness, gentleness and love, this meekness resulting from a humble heart, for love and gentleness are the greatest medicine for the fallen. He also warns the healer not to be proud lest he fall too, because we are no better than the one who fell.

entries.section: (1) Compassion for sinners

paragraphs.text: Bear ye one another's burdens: bearing the repeated sins and offenses of others, guiding them, visiting them, praying for them and offering every means of love to win them.

Love does not stop at not condemning the fallen, but goes on to bear their burdens and falls and to help them, as Christ bore our shame. This is the law of Christ, that is, His commandments which the Apostle Paul commanded us to fulfill.

Do we raise up the fallen with meekness and love, or are we harsh toward them?! Let us remember our sins, and so bear with them and encourage them, confident that continuing love softens the hardest rejecting hearts.

entries.section: (2) Let every man prove his own work

paragraphs.text: To be something: that is, he is proud and ascribes his works and glories to himself.

When he is nothing: considering that he is dust and ashes and falls into sins, and all his abilities are grace from God. Whoever is proud of the works he accomplishes, or his thoughts and words, forgetting that he is created from dust and that all his distinction is the work of God's grace in him, deceives himself, for he forgets his sins and weaknesses and steals God's glory for himself.

entries.section: (2) Let every man prove his own work

paragraphs.text: Let every man prove his own work: let him call himself to account before God and confess his sins before the priest. The Apostle Paul calls us to repentance instead of pride, so that man discovers his sins and is humbled and asks the help of God, who forgives him and supports him; and he boasts in the grace of God that supports him and is not proud toward others when he compares his good works with the shortcomings of others, because all these works are from God and not from himself.

entries.section: (2) Let every man prove his own work

paragraphs.text: In the end Paul affirms that every man is responsible for himself before God and will be called to account for all his works, so he should care for his repentance and not be occupied with comparing himself with others or being proud toward them, for this will not benefit him but will make him fall into sins that destroy him.
Be careful about your daily repentance before you sleep, for it cleanses you from all your sins and makes you humble before God, so you receive His mercies, and humble with people, so you win them.

entries.section: (3) Whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap

paragraphs.text: Communicate: he shares the material goods between himself and his teacher, giving him a part of them to meet his needs.

Christ declared that "the labourer is worthy of his hire" (Lk 10:7), and consequently whoever learns the word of God should care for his teacher's material needs and provide them for him. This fellowship establishes love between the two, and humility as well, for each of them needs the other and receives from him.

entries.section: (3) Whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap

paragraphs.text: Be not deceived: do not err and act in ignorance.
God is not mocked: no one can be proud against God by neglecting His commandments.
